summary: Describes how the LZS compression algorithm is used with the IP Payload Compression Protocol. It is a companion to the DEFLATE document and specifies how LZS-compressed data is carried. It is informational and does not define an Internet standard.

eli5.summary: LZS is another way to pack data into a smaller space, like folding clothes in a different way. This note explains how to use it to shrink data sent across the internet.

subtitle: How to squeeze IP packet payloads with the LZS compression algorithm, one datagram at a time.

tldr.problem: IPComp can compress IP datagram payloads, but it needs a concrete compression algorithm to plug in. This document supplies the LZS one.
tldr.mechanism: Each payload is compressed on its own with a freshly reset LZS history, and the compressor is flushed after every datagram so datagrams can arrive in any order.
tldr.outcome: This is an Informational document, not a standard. LZS is patented by Hi/fn, which offers licenses for a reference implementation.

today: RFC 2395 is an Informational document and the unit metadata shows no RFC obsoleting or updating it. It applies LZS to RFC 2393 (IPComp).

sections.title: Introduction and Background
sections.content:
RFC 2395 describes how to apply LZS, a lossless compression algorithm, to the payloads of IP datagrams. It is meant to be used together with the IP Payload Compression Protocol (IPComp), and it assumes the reader already understands IPComp.

LZS was developed by Hi/fn. It starts from a sliding-window history, similar to the classic Lempel-Ziv approach, and uses a window of 2,048 bytes. Redundant sequences are replaced by short tokens, and decompression recovers the original data exactly. Its encoding can compress strings as short as two octets.

The RFC notes that Hi/fn holds patents on LZS. Licenses for a reference implementation are available at no cost for IPPCP, IPSec, TLS and PPP uses, on a non-discriminatory basis.
sections.eli5: LZS finds parts of the data that repeat and swaps them for tiny shortcuts. When it unpacks, it gets back exactly what you started with, nothing lost.

sections.title: The Compression Process
sections.content:
The sender MUST reset the compression history before processing each datagram's payload. That way every payload can be decompressed on its own, which matters because datagrams can be received out of order.

The sender also MUST flush the compressor each time it sends a compressed datagram. Flushing means all the input goes into the output and nothing is held back hoping for better compression, so one datagram's data never spills into a later one.

The output payload holds the input data in either compressed or uncompressed form. If the uncompressed form is used, the output is identical to the input and the IPComp header is left out. If the compressed form is used, the output gets an IPComp header in front of it.
sections.eli5: Every packet is packed in its own fresh box and sealed completely. No packet ever needs another one to be opened, so they can arrive in any order.

sections.title: The LZS Encoding
sections.content:
Compressed data follows the ANSI X3.241-1994 encoding, which the RFC repeats for information only. A compressed stream is a series of compressed strings followed by an end marker. Each string is either a flag bit 0 followed by a raw 8-bit byte, or a flag bit 1 followed by an offset and a length that point back into earlier data.

An offset is either 7 bits (introduced by a 1) or 11 bits (introduced by a 0). Lengths use a variable-length code: 00 means 2, 01 means 3, 10 means 4, and longer matches use longer codes. The end marker is 110000000.

Because the payload always ends with the end marker, trailing bits and bytes after it can be treated as padding. The compressed payload must be a whole number of octets.
sections.eli5: The packed data is a list of two kinds of notes: "here is a plain letter" or "go back a bit and copy this many letters". A special stop note says where the list ends.

sections.title: IPComp Association Parameters
sections.content:
ISAKMP MAY be used to negotiate LZS for an IPComp association. The transform ID is IPCOMP_LZS, defined in the Internet IP Security Domain of Interpretation (RFC 2407). No other parameters are needed for LZS under ISAKMP. For manually configured associations, the CPI value IPCOMP_LZS is used.

Small packets may not compress well. Informal tests with LZS over the Calgary Corpus found that the average payload size that may produce expanded data is approximately 90 bytes, so implementations may not want to compress payloads smaller than that. LZS has no adaptive algorithm for compressibility testing.
sections.eli5: Two computers agree to use LZS by naming it in their setup chat. Tiny packets are not worth packing, because the box can end up bigger than the thing inside.

sections.title: Compression Efficiency by Datagram Size
sections.content: An appendix shows compression ratios achieved on the University of Calgary Text Compression Corpus, which has 18 files totaling 3.278MB, when LZS is applied to datagrams of different sizes. Bigger datagrams compress better: the ratio is 1.18 at 64 bytes and 2.14 at 16384 bytes.
sections.eli5: The more stuff you have in the box, the more repeats LZS can find, so big packets shrink more than tiny ones.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The document adds no security considerations beyond those already declared in IPComp and in the Deutsch96 reference it cites. Readers should look to those documents for the security discussion.
sections.eli5: Nothing new to worry about here. The safety notes live in the IPComp document.
